SOLARIS – Intelligent Health Monitoring for Astronauts

SOLARIS is an intelligent, interactive, and personalized health monitoring and decision-support platform designed to support astronauts during long-duration space missions, especially journeys to the Moon and Mars. When communication with Earth is delayed, astronauts need reliable ways to understand and monitor their health independently.

SOLARIS combines an intelligent voice assistant, interactive 3D human anatomy, personalized health analytics, and guided health assessments in one platform. It monitors health indicators, compares readings with individual baselines, highlights unusual changes, and explains findings in simple language. Its interactive 3D body helps astronauts understand how spaceflight conditions affect different body systems.

Built using React, TypeScript, Python, FastAPI, Three.js, and machine-learning technologies, SOLARIS follows a local-first approach designed to minimize dependence on cloud connectivity.

Our vision is to make astronaut healthcare more accessible, personalized, and understandable, supporting safer human exploration beyond Earth.
details:
SOLARIS – Intelligent Health Monitoring for Astronauts

Project Vision

When Earth is far away, understanding your health should never be out of reach.

1. What does SOLARIS do and how does it work?

Long-duration space missions expose astronauts to multiple health risks, including space radiation, microgravity, isolation, cardiovascular changes, bone density loss, immune system changes, sleep disruption, and psychological stress. During missions to the Moon and Mars, communication delays can make immediate medical assistance difficult. Astronauts therefore need reliable tools to understand and monitor their health independently.

SOLARIS is a voice-first, personalized astronaut health monitoring and decision-support platform designed to address this challenge. It transforms complex health measurements into understandable information by combining interactive 3D human anatomy, personalized health analytics, voice interaction, and guided health assessments in one unified system.

Its key capabilities include:

1. Intelligent Voice Assistant: Astronauts can interact with SOLARIS through voice or text, listen to health readings, ask questions, and complete verbal health check-ins. The assistant explains important findings in simple language, reducing dependence on complex screen navigation.

2. Personalized Health Intelligence: SOLARIS monitors health indicators such as heart rate, heart rate variability (HRV), SpO2, blood pressure, temperature, sleep, and other available measurements. It compares readings against individual health baselines, highlights unusual changes, and presents understandable status information.

3. Interactive 3D Human Anatomy: An interactive 3D human body allows astronauts to explore different body systems, understand their functions, view related health indicators, and learn how spaceflight conditions can affect their bodies.

4. Visual Health Analytics: Interactive charts, status indicators, historical trends, and a 30-day timeline help astronauts recognize changes over time instead of relying on isolated measurements.

5. Guided Health Assessment: SOLARIS includes guided measurement workflows, an Amsler grid-based vision self-screening feature, and verbal check-ins covering sleep, skin changes, spinal discomfort, and general well-being.

6. Exercise and Daily Health Management: The platform provides exercise countermeasure guidance, daily routines, and health reminders to encourage consistent self-monitoring and healthy habits.

7. Medical Review System: A dedicated review interface organizes astronaut health history and recorded findings to support medical personnel in reviewing health trends and potential concerns.

8. Mission Simulation: SOLARIS includes a simulator with clearly labeled fictional health and sensor data, allowing the complete monitoring experience to be demonstrated without requiring physical medical devices.

The platform combines deterministic health interpretation, statistical analysis, and experimental classical machine-learning components. It is designed around a local-first architecture, with essential local functionality intended to operate without continuous internet connectivity. SOLARIS is a research prototype and decision-support system, not a clinically validated medical device.

2. What benefits does it provide?

SOLARIS provides several important benefits for human space exploration:

  • Improved health awareness: Helps astronauts understand their health measurements and recognize unusual changes.
  • Personalized monitoring: Uses individual baselines to make health information more relevant to each astronaut.
  • Reduced interaction complexity: Voice-first communication makes health information easier to access during demanding mission activities.
  • Better visualization: Interactive 3D anatomy and analytics make complex physiological information easier to understand.
  • Support during communication delays: Provides local health information and self-monitoring capabilities when immediate communication with Earth is unavailable.
  • Medical review support: Organizes health records and trends for medical personnel.
  • Responsible technology: Clearly distinguishes simulated information, experimental model outputs, and actual measurements.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

Our primary goal is to contribute to safer, healthier, and more sustainable human exploration of the Moon and Mars.

SOLARIS aims to help astronauts become more informed about their own health, recognize potential concerns earlier, and maintain better health awareness throughout long-duration missions.

Its potential impact also extends beyond space exploration. Similar technology could support people working in isolated environments, including polar research stations, submarines, remote expeditions, and locations with limited access to healthcare.

Ultimately, we envision SOLARIS as a foundation for more personalized, accessible, and independent health monitoring in environments where traditional medical support is difficult to access.

4. What tools, programming languages, hardware, and software did we use?

We developed SOLARIS using a combination of modern web technologies, 3D visualization frameworks, local backend services, and scientific computing tools.

Frontend and Interface

  • React 18 and TypeScript
  • Vite
  • Tailwind CSS
  • React Router
  • Zustand
  • Framer Motion
  • Recharts

3D Visualization

  • Three.js
  • React Three Fiber
  • Drei
  • GLB-based 3D human anatomy model

Backend and Data Management

  • Python
  • FastAPI
  • SQLite
  • Pydantic

Machine Learning and Scientific Analysis

  • Scikit-learn
  • NumPy
  • Pandas
  • Joblib

Research Data

  • NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR), including Inspiration4 studies OSD-570 and OSD-571.
  • MMASH and Autonomic Aging datasets from PhysioNet.
  • Fictional and simulated astronaut profiles for demonstration.

Development Environment and Hardware

  • Visual Studio Code.
  • A standard laptop or desktop computer.
  • Microphone and speakers for voice interaction.
  • Simulated wearable and medical-device readings for demonstrations; no dedicated medical hardware is required.

5. What makes SOLARIS creative and innovative?

The innovation behind SOLARIS is its approach to transforming astronaut healthcare from passive data visualization into an interactive health intelligence experience.

Instead of simply displaying medical numbers, SOLARIS connects health measurements with personal baselines, explains their significance, and presents relevant information through voice interaction and interactive 3D anatomy.

Its distinguishing features are:

  • Voice-first healthcare: Makes health information accessible through natural interaction.
  • Personalized health interpretation: Focuses on individual physiological patterns rather than relying exclusively on general reference ranges.
  • 3D anatomical intelligence: Connects health indicators with the actual body systems they represent.
  • Spaceflight-aware monitoring: Relates health observations to the unique challenges of space exploration.
  • Local-first architecture: Prioritizes essential functionality without continuous dependence on cloud connectivity.
  • Transparent machine learning: Experimental models are clearly identified, and models showing unreliable performance or data leakage have been disabled.

By bringing these capabilities together, SOLARIS offers a more understandable and astronaut-centered approach to health monitoring than a conventional dashboard.

6. What factors did our team consider?

Our team considered the scientific, technical, operational, and human factors involved in developing health monitoring software for astronauts.

  1. Astronaut safety: Health information must be presented responsibly, with clear indications of potential concerns and appropriate escalation to medical personnel.
  2. Spaceflight conditions: The effects of radiation, microgravity, isolation, sleep disruption, and environmental conditions were considered.
  3. Communication delays: Essential health information should remain accessible without continuous communication with Earth.
  4. Data privacy: Personal astronaut health information requires appropriate access restrictions and privacy-conscious handling.
  5. Medical reliability: The system must distinguish between real measurements, simulated data, experimental predictions, and medically validated information.
  6. Usability and accessibility: The interface should be intuitive, visually understandable, and support voice and typed interaction.
  7. Computational efficiency: The architecture should remain practical for limited onboard computing resources.
  8. Future scalability: The system should allow future integration with real wearable sensors, medical devices, and additional mission environments.

Conclusion

SOLARIS represents our vision of making astronaut healthcare more intelligent, personalized, accessible, and independent.

By combining voice interaction, 3D human anatomy, individual health baselines, scientific analytics, and spaceflight-focused monitoring, we aim to help astronauts better understand their health when professional medical support from Earth is delayed.

SOLARIS – Because even millions of miles from Earth, every astronaut deserves to understand their health.
